summary: STRANDED: THE LAST ORBIT is a story-driven exploration game that utilizes an educational approach for the Space Mission Design Game Challenge. We follow the story of Laika, the Soviet space dog who became the first animal to orbit Earth aboard Sputnik 2. An imagined journey from Earth’s orbit to the Moon and Mars, where players must manage Laika’s oxygen and food supplies while protecting the spacecraft from threats such as space debris. Real NASA history and orbital data appear as discoverable facts, showing why Sputnik 2’s mission was a one-way journey and highlighting Laika’s impact on future space exploration, not only around Earth but beyond, throughout the solar system. But before we look toward the future of space exploration, let us see the universe through Laika’s eyes and discover how she managed to survive in Earth’s outer orbit.
details:
Rambot’s Project Solution

  • History sent Laika on a one-way mission. We never forgot it. STRANDED: THE LAST ORBIT is an educational mission-design game built in Godot 4.7.2 with GDScript that turns that real Sputnik 2 flight into a playable second chance. Players take command, configuring the capsule, choosing instruments, and balancing mass, power, fuel, oxygen, food, and signal across launch, orbit, and a fictional voyage to the Moon and Mars, where every choice is a trade-off, every failure is explained, and the final report reveals what was real and what was mercy. It is built on NASA mission-design resources and verified Sputnik 2 history, with NASA's GMAT validating the physics, for students and space enthusiasts who learn best through story and consequence.

How our game actually has showcased and provided the solution 

  • Phase 1: The real orbit. Players begin aboard Sputnik 2, launching on November 3, 1957, from Baikonur. They discover the mission’s real numbers behind the orbit. Between 212 km and 1,660 km above the earth, one lap every 103.7 minutes, and a 508.3 kg capsule, which was Laika, located. These are the anchors the rest of the game must respect.

Sputnik 2 ground-track and telemetry passes.
From https://youtu.be/OgCcLcixnxU?si=qoYJGSY_Uip_tEsE

  • Phase 2: The reality and fiction. Players learn Sputnik 2 moved at 8.16 km/s at its lowest point, while escaping Earth from there required 11.0 km/s. The capsule had no engine to close that 2.9 km/s gap and no way to land or relaunch anywhere. We validated the physics with three what-if burns in NASA's GMAT with no push, +1.5 km/s, and +2.9 km/s that produce a closed orbit, a larger closed orbit, and escape, matching our hand calculations. So the game does not pretend the voyage is physically possible. It names its one impossibility: Echo, the voice that answers Laika in the dark, is the miracle that carries her beyond Earth orbit. Everything past that point is presented as fiction, and the ending reveals what the miracle was for.

GMAT baseline: no burn, closed orbit around Earth.

GMAT +2.9 km/s: trajectory escapes Earth.

GMAT +1.5 km/s: larger but still closed orbit.

  • Phase 3: The imagined voyage. With the physics anchored and the one impossibility named, the story diverges into Earth to Moon, then to Mars, and finally back to Earth. Players need to configure the capsule through the challenge's trade-offs, like coolers vs. fuel vs. sensor and relay vs. fuel, then manage oxygen, food, power, and signal across 663.9 million km and roughly 2.85 years. Longer legs cost more supplies and more exposure to debris; the asteroid and resource minigames make those costs physical, and every advantage is paid for elsewhere. Echo is the only reason the ship can land and launch again; the game never pretends otherwise. Along the way, real facts surface as discoverables: moon dust, Mawrth Vallis, the thin Martian air, and the physics of a suit running out of seals.

NASA Mars Trek view of Mawrth Vallis, used as the Mars landing/terrain reference.

  • Phase 4: The evaluation and the real ending. Every run closes with a mission report: resources remaining, launch attempts, hazards survived, objects found, retries, and a plain-language explanation of which decision caused the outcome of the challenge's why-did-it-fail feedback, delivered in-game. Then the game returns to history: Laika died of overheating hours after launch; Sputnik 2's batteries failed on 10 November 1957, and it re-entered on 14 April 1958. The final screen separates verified history from the fiction we invented and closes by remembering Laika not as a footnote, but as the reason the mission matters. The voyage was Echo's mercy; the report is ours.

Trade-offs

  • Every good choice costs something. The Moon-to-Mars leg is the biggest risk: at 7.39 km/s it lasts about 519 days, against 13 hours for Earth-to-Moon, so oxygen and food burn while debris exposure piles up. Players will need to push the speed up and avoid any asteroids in their way to Mars.

A real trade-off from history 

  • Sputnik 2 was reportedly rushed to launch around the Bolshevik Revolution anniversary (Grechko interview) and built to reach orbit, not return with no engine, no recovery plan. Reports say the R-7 sustainer failed to separate, disrupting thermal control, and the cabin overheated within five to six hours. The schedule was traded against safety margin and recovery.

Facts vs. Fiction

  • The physics is real; the story adds exactly one impossibility. Sputnik 2's launch, 212 × 1,660 km orbit, 508.3 kg capsule, Laika's death by hyperthermia, and the April 1958 re-entry are verified history. The Moon–Mars voyage, Laika's survival, and Echo: the voice that enables it are labeled fiction. Every real number is traceable to NASA data, GMAT validated the one-way result as a development check, and the final report separates what happened from what we imagined. Full research, sources, and GMAT runs: website link.

The Game Benefits

STRANDED turns the challenge's educational goals into player outcomes:

  • Systems thinking: every run moves through the full pipeline objective, requirements, spacecraft, instruments, launch/orbit, operations, evaluation so players see how one decision propagates.
  • Resource literacy: players learn mass, power, fuel, oxygen, food, signal, and heat by spending them, not memorizing definitions.
  • Failure that teaches: the mission report explains why a run failed and which earlier choice caused it, matching the challenge's why-did-it-fail requirement.
  • Historical literacy and ethics: Laika's verified story anchors the game, and the fact/fiction split teaches responsible science communication.
  • Accessibility: plain-language dialogue, visual indicators, and short sessions make mission design approachable for students and non-experts.
  • Replayability: different capsule and instrument picks produce different reports, inviting experimentation and comparison.
  • The result: players learn integrated mission design through decisions, constraints, and consequences and remember the cost because the story makes them care.

Our goal

  • To make NASA's open data and space history more accessible, helping students and non-experts understand the trade-offs, limits, and hard choices behind real space missions while fostering awareness of the human side of exploration. Despite our attempt to represent a complete mission, our game is limited to one historical mission and a small set of decisions; it does not cover other mission types, launch vehicles, or orbital regimes, and it simplifies real trajectories for playability.

Tools and Technologies Used

Coding Languages:

  • GDScript → for 2D game development in Godot Engine 4.7.
  • Python → for asset processing and research data extraction (development support).

Data Sources:

  • NASA History Division → verified Sputnik 2/Laika facts used in the opening disclaimer, Jin's dialogue, and trivia.
  • NASA "Design and Develop Science Missions" (2025) → mission-design pipeline and four mission segments that shape the game's structure.
  • NASA/JPL "Concept Maturity Levels" → framing that early design decisions constrain later choices in the mission report.
  • NASA Webb "Build It Yourself" → inspiration for objective-gated choices and the final comparison to a real NASA mission.

Character Design

  • Aseprite → for creating and editing pixel-style sprites, animations, tilesets, and splash art for Laika, Jin, and the ship.
